college.stem: A hiker sees dark clouds and a falling barometer, concludes that a storm is probably coming, and then picks the shorter of two trails. How should these two mental steps be labeled?
options: Concluding that a storm is likely is reasoning, and picking a trail is decision making.
Concluding that a storm is likely is decision making, and picking a trail is reasoning.
Both steps are reasoning, because any choice between trails is simply another conclusion.
Neither step involves a judgment, because judgments happen only after an action is complete.
college.why: Reasoning is drawing conclusions and decision making is choosing between alternatives, so the storm conclusion is reasoning that then guides the trail choice. Swapping or merging the labels ignores that distinction.

simple.stem: What is the difference between reasoning and decision making?
options: Reasoning draws conclusions, while decision making chooses between alternatives.
Reasoning chooses between alternatives, while decision making draws conclusions.
Reasoning relies on memory, while decision making never relies on memory.
They are two names for exactly the same mental process.
simple.why: Reasoning is the process of drawing conclusions; decision making is the process of choosing between alternatives. The reversed option swaps the two definitions.

college.stem: A survey team collects 5,000 opinions, all from residents of one wealthy neighborhood, and claims that the sheer number makes its conclusion about the whole city certain. Which evaluation fits inductive reasoning?
options: The conclusion is still only probable, and its strength depends on representativeness and quality as well as number.
Five thousand observations are enough to make an inductive conclusion about the entire city definitely and permanently true.
Representativeness matters only when a conclusion rests on a single observation rather than on many.
Only the count of observations matters, so their source and their quality can be safely ignored.
college.why: Inductive conclusions are probably, not definitely, true, and their strength depends on the representativeness, number and quality of the observations. A large but unrepresentative sample does not produce certainty.

simple.stem: Which factors determine how strong an inductive argument is?
options: How representative, how numerous, and how high in quality the observations are.
Only how many observations were collected, regardless of anything else about them.
Only how confident the person feels about the conclusion that was reached.
Whether the conclusion follows with complete certainty from its starting premises.
simple.why: The strength of an inductive argument depends on the representativeness, number and quality of observations. Number alone is not enough, and inductive conclusions are never fully certain.

college.stem: A traveler has seen hundreds of white swans and concludes that all swans are white. She then clearly observes one black swan. Why can this single observation outweigh the many earlier ones?
options: A clear, high-quality observation directly contradicts the universal claim, however many white swans came before it.
A single observation always supports a generalization more strongly than any large set of observations does.
The black swan matters only if black swans outnumber white swans in the group she has observed.
Inductive reasoning requires setting aside any unusual observation whenever it conflicts with a large body of past experience.
college.why: The quality of observations, not just their number, affects the strength of an inductive argument, and one compelling observation can carry a lot of weight. A reliable counter-instance directly undercuts the claim that every swan is white.

simple.stem: Why can one very convincing observation carry a lot of weight in inductive reasoning?
options: Because the quality of an observation, not just the number, affects argument strength.
Because inductive conclusions are always based on exactly one observation.
Because the number of observations never matters in inductive reasoning.
Because one strong observation makes any inductive conclusion definitely and permanently true.
simple.why: Argument strength depends on quality as well as number, so one compelling, high-quality observation can matter a great deal. It still does not make an inductive conclusion certain.

college.stem: Which statement best captures how inductive reasoning operates in everyday life?
options: It uses what happened in the past to predict what will happen now, sometimes automatically in familiar situations.
It counts only when a person deliberately writes out every relevant past observation in a list before making any choice at all.
It guides behavior only when the current situation has nothing in common with earlier situations.
It guarantees that an outcome observed in the past will occur again in every future instance.
college.why: Inductive reasoning lets past experience guide present behavior, especially in familiar situations, and some of it happens automatically. Its predictions are probable, not guaranteed.

simple.stem: How do people use inductive reasoning in everyday life?
options: They predict what will happen based on what has happened before.
They avoid using past experience when they make predictions.
They reason this way only when solving formal logic problems.
They reach conclusions that are guaranteed to be true every time.
simple.why: Everyday induction uses past experience to predict what will happen, often in familiar situations. Its conclusions are likely rather than guaranteed.

college.stem: A mental shortcut usually gives a fast, correct answer, but occasionally it leads a person astray. Which definition of a heuristic fits both outcomes?
options: A rule of thumb that is likely to give the correct answer quickly but is not foolproof.
An exhaustive procedure that guarantees a correct answer whenever past experience is used.
A random guess that does not draw on any information stored in memory at all.
A reasoning error by definition, so a correct answer could never have come from one.
college.why: Heuristics are rules of thumb that help people reach conclusions rapidly and are likely, but not certain, to be correct. That is why the same shortcut can succeed in one case and fail in another.

simple.stem: What is a heuristic?
options: A rule of thumb that is often right but not foolproof.
A step-by-step method that always gives the correct answer.
A random guess made without using any past experience.
A type of reasoning error that is always wrong.
simple.why: A heuristic is a shortcut that is likely to give the right answer but can fail. It is neither guaranteed correct nor always wrong.

college.stem: Two kinds of events happen equally often, but one is emotionally vivid and the person has recalled it many times. The person judges the vivid event more probable because instances come to mind easily. What explains this judgment?
options: The availability heuristic, since emotion and repeated retrieval make instances easier to recall without making them more frequent.
The representativeness heuristic, since the person judges the event by comparing it with the most typical member of a familiar occupational category.
The law of large numbers, since the most emotional event must also be the most frequent one.
The conjunction rule, since an event recalled repeatedly becomes more probable than its original occurrence.
college.why: Under the availability heuristic, events that are easier to remember are judged more probable, and emotional salience and repeated retrieval make events stand out in memory. Representativeness concerns resemblance to a category, not ease of recall.

simple.stem: What is the availability heuristic?
options: Judging events that are easier to remember as more probable.
Judging how likely something is by how well it matches a category.
Judging a combination of two events as more likely than either alone.
Judging probability by carefully counting how often each event occurs.
simple.why: The availability heuristic treats ease of recall as a sign of probability. Matching a category describes representativeness instead.

college.stem: When asked whether more English words begin with r or have r as the third letter, about 70% say words beginning with r, although words with r third are about three times more common. What best explains the error?
options: Words are easier to retrieve by their first letter, and that ease of recall is mistaken for higher frequency.
People know the true frequency ratio but reverse it when asked to give a category label instead.
People wrongly believe that every English word contains the letter r in both of those positions.
An easier retrieval cue actually changes how many words that begin with the letter r exist in the English language.
college.why: It is easier to call to mind words by their first letter, so r-first words are more available and are judged more common. The actual frequencies favor r in the third position.

simple.stem: Most people say more English words start with r than have r in third place. Why is this judgment wrong?
options: Words with r third are more common, but words starting with r are easier to recall.
Words starting with r are rarer, and people confuse r with similar-looking letters.
Both kinds of words are equally common, so neither answer is better than the other.
People judge correctly but misunderstand which letter position they were asked about.
simple.why: About three times more words have r in the third position, but words starting with r come to mind more easily. That ease of recall is the availability heuristic at work.

college.stem: Asked whether a randomly chosen person in the United States is more likely to die next year of asthma or of botulism, many people pick botulism, although asthma deaths are far more common. Why?
options: Botulism deaths make front-page news while asthma deaths go unnoticed, so botulism is more available.
Botulism resembles a typical cause of death more closely, so representativeness overrides the asthma base rate.
People correctly judge botulism as more frequent, because news coverage mirrors how often each cause occurs.
People apply the conjunction rule, which makes a rare single cause seem more probable than a common one.
college.why: The cause-of-death errors reflect availability: dramatic botulism deaths are front-page news, whereas asthma deaths go virtually unnoticed. News coverage reflects salience, not actual frequency.

simple.stem: Why do people often judge death from botulism as more likely than death from asthma?
options: Botulism deaths get big news coverage, so they come to mind more easily.
Botulism really does kill more people each year than asthma does.
Botulism better matches people's idea of a typical deadly illness.
People are given the true death rates and simply misremember them.
simple.why: Botulism deaths are front-page news while asthma deaths go virtually unnoticed, so botulism is more available in memory. In fact asthma causes far more deaths.

college.stem: The United States has about 2.2 million farms and 120,000 libraries. Robert, a randomly chosen man, wears glasses, speaks quietly, and reads a lot. Most people say he is more likely a librarian. What makes this a representativeness error?
options: His description matches the typical librarian, and that similarity leads people to ignore how many more farmers there are.
People recall every librarian they have personally met and count those remembered instances one by one.
The judgment depends on a conjunction of two nested categories, like the feminist bank tellers.
The description changes the actual numbers of farms and libraries, so that librarians now outnumber farmers in the population.
college.why: Representativeness judges membership by resemblance to a category, and here the resemblance leads people to ignore the base rate of farmers versus librarians. Counting recalled instances would be availability, and the base rates themselves do not change.

simple.stem: What is the representativeness heuristic?
options: Judging whether something belongs to a group by how much it resembles that group.
Judging how likely an event is by how easily instances of that event come to mind.
Judging that larger samples are more representative than smaller samples.
Judging a claim true only after collecting many high-quality observations.
simple.why: The representativeness heuristic bases judgments on how closely one thing resembles a category. Ease of recall describes the availability heuristic.

college.stem: In a group of 100 people with 70 lawyers and 30 engineers, participants correctly estimate the chance of drawing an engineer. After learning that Jack enjoys carpentry, sailing, and mathematical puzzles, they say Jack is an engineer. What does the change in responses show?
options: People use base rates when that is all they have but disregard them once descriptive information is available.
People cannot understand numerical probability at all, which is also why they fail the bare question about lawyers and engineers.
Adding the description actually changes the group into 70 engineers and 30 lawyers.
The description has no effect, because both questions use exactly the same occupation labels.
college.why: People answer the base-rate-only question correctly, but once a fitting description appears they rely on it and disregard the base rate. The group composition never changes.

simple.stem: In the lawyer-engineer problem, how do people's answers change once a description of Jack is added?
options: They stop using the 70-to-30 base rate and go by the description.
They start using the base rate, which they had ignored before.
Their answers stay the same, because the base rate has not changed.
They refuse to answer, because the description seems irrelevant to them.
simple.why: With only the base rate, people answer correctly; with a description that fits an engineer, they disregard the base rate and say Jack is an engineer.

college.stem: A respondent rates “Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement” as more probable than “Linda is a bank teller.” Why does this ranking violate the conjunction rule?
options: Every feminist bank teller is also a bank teller, so adding a condition cannot raise the probability.
Every bank teller is necessarily a feminist, so the two statements carry identical information.
A statement with more matching personality details is always more probable than a shorter one.
The conjunction rule applies only when the two categories share no members at all.
college.why: The probability of two events together cannot exceed the probability of either one alone, and feminist bank tellers are a subset of bank tellers. A good descriptive fit does not change that.

simple.stem: What does the conjunction rule state?
options: Two events together cannot be more probable than either one alone.
Two events together are always more probable than either one alone.
Two events together are exactly as probable as each one alone.
Detailed descriptions are more probable than short, general descriptions.
simple.why: The conjunction rule says the probability of two events together cannot be higher than the probability of each single event.

college.stem: A town's larger hospital has about 45 births a day and its smaller hospital about 15. For a year, each records the days on which more than 60% of the babies born were boys. What must be compared to decide which hospital records more such days?
options: How often each hospital's daily sample yields an extreme percentage, given its daily sample size.
The total number of boys each hospital delivers across the full year of records.
Nothing at all, since both daily samples must contain exactly 50% boys like the population.
Only the number of births, because a bigger hospital produces more of every kind of day.
college.why: The question concerns how often a daily proportion crosses a 60% threshold, which depends on daily sample size. Annual totals of boys do not answer it.

simple.stem: In the hospital problem (15 versus 45 births a day), how did most people answer?
options: Most said both hospitals would record about the same number of days.
Most said the larger hospital would record more such days.
Most said the smaller hospital would record more such days.
Most said neither hospital would ever record such a day.
simple.why: 56% answered “about the same,” with 22% each choosing the larger or the smaller hospital. The correct answer, the smaller hospital, was picked by only a minority.

college.stem: In the hospital problem, both hospitals draw from a population that is about half boys. Why should the hospital with 15 daily births record more days above 60% boys than the one with 45?
options: Smaller daily samples vary more, so their proportions stray from the population value more often.
Fewer births a day means the underlying population of babies must contain more boys.
The smaller hospital has more total births, so each of its daily percentages is higher.
The larger hospital can never exceed 60% boys, because large samples remove all random day-to-day variation.
college.why: Small samples fluctuate more, so the smaller hospital more often departs from 50% boys. The population proportion is the same for both, and large samples still vary somewhat.

simple.stem: Which hospital records more days with over 60% boys, and why?
options: The smaller hospital, because small samples swing away from 50% more often.
The larger hospital, because it has more babies born each day.
Both equally, because each hospital's population of newborns is about half boys.
Neither, because over 60% boys can never happen on any day.
simple.why: The correct answer is the smaller hospital: small samples are less representative of the population, so extreme days are more common there.

college.stem: Which statement expresses the law of large numbers?
options: The more individuals randomly drawn from a population, the more representative the group tends to be.
Every random sample exactly reproduces its population as soon as the first individual is selected.
Increasing the size of a sample guarantees that every individual observation has an identical value.
Random selection makes sample size irrelevant to how closely a group resembles its population.
college.why: The law of large numbers says larger random samples are more representative of the population. Small random samples can still depart substantially from it.

simple.stem: What error do people make about small samples?
options: They assume small samples represent the population as well as large ones.
They assume small samples are less accurate than any single observation.
They assume small samples must contain only extreme or unusual cases.
They assume small samples can never be drawn at random from any population.
simple.why: People often assume representativeness holds for small samples, which leads to reasoning errors. By the law of large numbers, larger samples are the more representative ones.

college.stem: Someone holding a stereotype notices and remembers behaviors that fit it, overlooks behaviors that do not, and concludes that the group and the behavior are strongly linked. What process is at work?
options: Selective attention makes fitting behaviors more available, creating an illusory correlation that reinforces the stereotype.
An accurate correlation has been measured from a representative and unbiased sample of the group's full range of everyday behavior.
The stereotype keeps fitting behaviors out of memory entirely, so availability plays no role at all.
The conjunction rule shows that a group must display every behavior that is attributed to it.
college.why: Attention to stereotype-consistent behaviors makes them more available, producing an illusory correlation that reinforces the stereotype. The perceived link is absent or weaker than assumed, not accurately measured.

simple.stem: What is an illusory correlation?
options: A relationship that seems to exist but is absent or much weaker than assumed.
A real relationship that has been measured accurately in a large sample.
A relationship that people notice only after it has been proven statistically.
A relationship between two events that always happen at exactly the same time.
simple.why: An illusory correlation is a perceived relationship that does not exist or is much weaker than people assume. It often arises when people expect two things to be related.

college.stem: Lord and colleagues (1979) had people who favored and people who opposed capital punishment read the same article. Supporters judged the article as favoring their view, and opponents judged it as opposing theirs. What does giving both groups the same article establish?
options: Prior attitudes can steer how identical information is judged, with each side focusing on what agreed with it.
The two groups must have received different articles, since a single article cannot be interpreted in two opposite ways.
Exposure to identical evidence removes any influence of prior beliefs on how that evidence is judged.
Myside bias appears only when participants are prevented from seeing any information about the issue.
college.why: Because the evidence was identical, the opposite evaluations must come from the readers' attitudes: each side focused on agreeing information and disregarded the rest. This is the myside bias.

simple.stem: In the study by Lord and colleagues (1979), what happened when supporters and opponents of capital punishment read the same article?
options: Each side judged the article as supporting its own view.
Both sides judged the article as supporting capital punishment.
Both sides changed their minds after seeing the evidence.
Neither side found the article related to the issue at all.
simple.why: Those in favor found the article in favor and those against found it against, showing the myside bias. Neither side changed its mind.

college.stem: In the 2, 4, 6 number-rule task, a participant keeps testing triples that increase by two, such as 8, 10, 12, and is told each one fits the rule. Why does this feedback fail to confirm the participant's hypothesis?
options: Those triples also fit the broader actual rule of any three increasing numbers, so they cannot tell the rules apart.
Positive feedback means the experimenter has confirmed the participant's stated rule in every detail.
The actual rule requires decreasing numbers, so every increasing triple should have been rejected.
The feedback reports whether the participant has found a new mathematical law, rather than whether a particular triple fits the rule.
college.why: Feedback only says whether a triple fits the hidden rule, which was any three numbers in increasing order. Triples increasing by two fit both that rule and the narrower hypothesis, so they cannot distinguish them.

simple.stem: In the 2, 4, 6 number-rule task, what was the actual rule?
options: Any three numbers in increasing order of magnitude.
Three even numbers that increase by two each time.
Any three numbers that add up to an even number.
Three numbers in which the last equals the sum of the others.
simple.why: The actual rule was simply three numbers in increasing order. The most common hypothesis, increasing intervals of two, was too narrow.

college.stem: Under expected utility theory, what will a rational person who has all the relevant information choose?
options: The option that yields the maximum expected utility, such as the greatest expected monetary payoff.
The option with the single largest possible prize, whatever its chance of actually occurring.
The option containing the most favorable items, regardless of how many items there are in total.
The option most recently retrieved from memory, even if its expected benefit is lower.
college.why: Expected utility theory assumes people are rational and, with all relevant information, choose the option with maximum expected utility, such as maximum monetary payoff. The biggest possible prize ignores its probability.

simple.stem: What does expected utility theory assume about people?
options: They are rational and choose whatever gives the maximum expected utility.
They are emotional and choose whatever option feels safest to them at the moment.
They rely on heuristics and choose whatever comes to mind first.
They ignore payoffs and choose whatever other people are choosing.
simple.why: The theory assumes rational decision makers who, given all relevant information, maximize expected utility. Relying on heuristics is what the theory leaves out.

college.stem: A person who knows that casino odds are heavily against them still decides to gamble. What problem does this pose for the utility approach?
options: Many choices do not maximize the chance of the best outcome, and people value more than money.
It shows that anyone who chooses to gamble at a casino must be unaware of the odds against winning.
It shows that the expected monetary payoff of casino gambling is actually positive.
It shows that every outcome people value must be converted into equal sums of money.
college.why: People gamble even though they know the odds are against them, so they are not utility-maximization machines and may find value in things other than money. Knowing the odds does not stop the choice.

simple.stem: Which is a problem for the utility approach to decision making?
options: People often make choices that do not maximize their expected payoff.
It provides no procedure at all for identifying the best choice.
People always choose the option with the highest monetary payoff.
People are perfectly consistent in every decision they make.
simple.why: A key problem is that many decisions do not maximize the best outcome, as when people gamble despite bad odds. Having specific procedures for the best choice is an advantage of the approach, not a problem.

college.stem: Participants could earn $1 for each red jellybean drawn and chose between a bowl with 1 red bean in 10 and a bowl with 7 red beans in 100. Most chose the 7-in-100 bowl. What does a correct comparison of the bowls show?
options: Seven red beans is the larger count, but 7 out of 100 is a lower chance than 1 out of 10.
Seven red beans gives a 70% chance, since each bowl should be treated as holding ten beans.
The bowls offer equal chances, because each one contains at least one red jellybean.
The bowl with more beans in total always offers the better chance, whatever their colors.
college.why: The chances are 10% versus 7%, so the popular bowl is worse; the larger number of red beans draws attention away from the larger total. This is why the choice was influenced by considerations other than probabilities.

simple.stem: In the jellybean study, most participants chose the bowl with 7 red beans out of 100 instead of 1 out of 10. What does this show?
options: Their choices were influenced by considerations other than probabilities.
They correctly picked the bowl with the better chance of winning.
They could not tell the red jellybeans from the white ones.
They preferred to earn as little money as they possibly could.
simple.why: The 7-in-100 bowl has worse odds than 1-in-10, so choosing it shows that something other than probability guided the decision.

college.stem: After September 11, 2001, air travel decreased and driving increased. Why could this shift in behavior be harmful?
options: Dying in a car accident is far more likely than dying in a flight, so drivers faced greater danger.
Switching to a different mode of travel removes any possibility of dying on the journey itself.
A frightening event is, by definition, more probable than a less noticeable kind of event.
Risk depends only on whether a person has personally witnessed a crash of that particular type.
college.why: The probability of dying in a car accident is far greater than in flying, so avoiding a salient threat raised exposure to a likelier one. Salience does not make an event more probable.

simple.stem: What happened after 9/11, when many Americans drove instead of flying?
options: More people died on the roads than were killed on the hijacked flights.
Road deaths fell, because people drove more carefully than before.
Air travel became riskier than driving for the following few years after the attacks.
The number of people traveling by car did not change at all.
simple.why: The number of Americans who died on the road to avoid flying was higher than the total number of passengers killed on the four hijacked flights.

college.stem: In Ritov and Baron's (1999) convoy dilemma, rerouting food trucks to a second camp would save 1,000 people but cause 100 deaths at the first camp. Sixty-three percent refused to reroute. What does this response suggest?
options: A larger net number of lives saved does not by itself decide whether people take an action that harms others.
Respondents were maximizing the net number of lives saved, since refusing to reroute actually saves more people in total.
Rerouting would save no one at the second camp, so the two options had identical outcomes.
Respondents saw the two routes as identical, with no difference in who would receive the food.
college.why: Rerouting has the better net balance (1,000 saved versus 100 lost), yet 63% refused. Their choice therefore rests on something beyond maximizing the net count of lives.

simple.stem: In Ritov and Baron's (1999) convoy dilemma, what did most people decide?
options: They would not send the convoy to the second camp.
They would send the convoy to the second camp.
They would split the convoy between the two camps.
They would send the convoy back without delivering food.
simple.why: 63% did not choose to send the convoy to the second camp, even though rerouting would save 1,000 people at a cost of 100.

college.stem: In Tetlock and colleagues' (2000) Sacred Value Protection Model, how do taboo and tragic tradeoffs differ?
options: A taboo tradeoff mixes a sacred value with a secular one, while a tragic tradeoff pits two sacred values against each other.
A taboo tradeoff pits two sacred values against each other, while a tragic tradeoff sets a sacred value against an amount of money.
Both involve offers that are too small, and they do not differ in the kinds of values being compared.
Both are defined by a willingness to exchange sacred values for the largest payment that is available.
college.why: Mixing the sacred and secular domains is taboo and triggers moral outrage; comparing two sacred values is tragic and produces less outrage. The second option reverses the two terms.

simple.stem: In Tetlock and colleagues' (2000) model, how do people respond when a sacred value is traded against a secular value such as money?
options: They feel threatened and respond with moral outrage.
They feel relieved and respond with gratitude toward the decider.
They feel nothing, because secular values never matter to them.
They see it as a tragic choice and feel little outrage.
simple.why: When sacred and secular values are mixed, people feel threatened and respond with moral outrage, which makes it a taboo tradeoff. Little outrage goes with tragic tradeoffs between two sacred values.

college.stem: In the scenario used by Tetlock and colleagues (2000), Robert can save five-year-old Johnny with a liver transplant or spend its $1,000,000 cost on other hospital needs. Which change would turn this taboo tradeoff into a tragic one?
options: Replacing the hospital spending with a second child who needs the only available liver.
Raising the amount of money at stake while keeping the choice between money and Johnny's life.
Keeping both options the same but describing the hospital budget in much greater detail.
Removing Johnny's need for a transplant, so that no life depends on either of the options.
college.why: The tragic scenario has two children needing a transplant and only one liver, pitting a sacred value against another sacred value. Changing the amount of money keeps a sacred-versus-secular, taboo tradeoff.

simple.stem: In Tetlock and colleagues' (2000) tragic tradeoff scenario, what choice did the decision maker face?
options: Two children needed a liver transplant, but only one liver was available.
One child's transplant competed with spending money on hospital equipment.
A hospital had to choose between two expensive pieces of new equipment.
A doctor had to choose between two higher salaries for new staff.
simple.why: The tragic scenario involves two children who need a liver transplant but only one liver. A child's life versus hospital spending is the taboo scenario.

college.stem: Which pattern of moral outrage did Tetlock and colleagues (2000) find for decisions about saving Johnny?
options: Under taboo, not saving Johnny drew far more outrage than saving him; under tragic, both outcomes drew similar outrage.
Saving Johnny drew more outrage than not saving him, and by an equal margin in both kinds of tradeoff.
The tragic tradeoff showed the same large difference between saving and not saving him as the taboo one did.
Outrage depended only on whether Johnny survived and was unaffected by which type of tradeoff was involved.
college.why: In the taboo condition, outrage was about 5.4 when Johnny was not saved versus about 2.4 when he was saved; in the tragic condition both outcomes were near 3.8. So tradeoff type changed the effect of the outcome.

simple.stem: In Tetlock and colleagues' (2000) results, when was moral outrage highest?
options: When Johnny was not saved in the taboo tradeoff.
When Johnny was saved in the taboo tradeoff.
When Johnny was not saved in the tragic tradeoff.
When Johnny was saved in the tragic tradeoff.
simple.why: Outrage was highest (about 5.4 on the scale) when Johnny was not saved in the taboo tradeoff, where money competed with his life. In the tragic tradeoff, the two outcomes drew similar outrage.

college.stem: Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (2007) interviewed Israeli settlers, Palestinian refugees, and Palestinian students affiliated with political groups about possible peace deals. What set this research apart from earlier work?
options: It extended sacred-value findings to a realistic setting, with conflict-involved groups judging real issues.
It tested randomly chosen laboratory volunteers who had no personal, political, or historical connection to the conflict at all.
It measured only memory for word lists and never asked about any proposed tradeoff.
It assumed every participant held identical sacred values because all came from one group.
college.why: The study extended previous findings to a more realistic setting by asking people involved in the conflict about tradeoff deals. It did not assume all of them held the issues as sacred.

simple.stem: Whom did Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (2007) interview?
options: Israeli settlers, Palestinian refugees, and Palestinian students.
American college students recruited for a laboratory study.
Government negotiators from several countries in the region.
Iranian participants who completed an online survey written in Farsi.
simple.why: The study interviewed Israeli settlers (n = 601), Palestinian refugees (n = 535) and politically affiliated Palestinian students (719). The online Farsi survey belongs to the Iranian nuclear studies.

college.stem: In the deals proposed by Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (2007), how does the Symbolic offer differ from the Taboo+ offer?
options: The Symbolic offer adds Israeli recognition of Palestinian rights and an apology, while Taboo+ adds a yearly payment.
The Symbolic offer adds a larger yearly payment to Palestine, while Taboo+ contains no monetary term of any kind at all.
Both offers keep identical terms and differ only in the wording used to introduce each of them.
The Symbolic offer removes all recognition of historical claims from the basic two-state agreement.
college.why: Taboo+ adds a payment of 1 billion U.S. dollars a year for 10 years, while the Symbolic offer adds Israel's recognition of the Palestinians' right to a state and an apology. One is monetary, the other symbolic.

simple.stem: In the Taboo+ deal of Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (2007), what was added to the basic deal?
options: Israel would pay Palestine $1 billion a year for 10 years.
Israel would apologize for all wrongs done to the Palestinians.
Israel would give up its claim to all of Jerusalem.
The United Nations would impose sanctions on both sides.
simple.why: Taboo+ added a monetary payment of $1 billion a year for 10 years. The apology belongs to the Symbolic offer.

college.stem: Two participants in the study by Ginges and colleagues (2007) strongly oppose giving up land. One says it is never permissible no matter how great the benefit; the other would weigh the benefits. How does the sacred-value measure sort them?
options: Only the first counts as a moral absolutist; strong opposition by itself does not make a value sacred.
Both count as moral absolutists, because any strong preference is the same thing as a sacred value.
The second counts as the absolutist, because sacred values are the ones that maximize monetary gain.
Neither can hold a sacred value, because the measure requires indifference to the disputed issue.
college.why: Moral absolutists refuse compromise no matter how great the benefit, whereas non-absolutists can strongly oppose compromise without treating the issue as sacred. Strength of preference alone does not decide the category.

simple.stem: In the study by Ginges and colleagues (2007), who counted as a moral absolutist?
options: Someone who would never compromise on the issue, no matter the benefit.
Someone who strongly dislikes compromise but would consider large benefits.
Someone who has no strong opinion about the disputed issue at all.
Someone who would accept any deal that offered enough money.
simple.why: Moral absolutists turned the disputed issues into sacred values that could never be given up, however great the benefit. Strong opposition that still weighs benefits marks a non-absolutist.

college.stem: In the results of Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (2007), adding money to a taboo deal (Taboo+) increased anger and disgust among moral absolutists but slightly decreased it among non-absolutists. What does this imply?
options: A monetary offer's effect depends on whether the issue is held as sacred; money has no single uniform effect.
Monetary additions are always welcomed by every group of participants, as long as the amount offered is positive.
Absolutists and non-absolutists changed in identical ways, so sacred status made no difference.
The monetary addition turned every participant's preference into a sacred value before the ratings.
college.why: The same added money moved the two groups in opposite directions, so its effect depends on sacred-value status. For moral absolutists the incentive backfired.

simple.stem: In the results of Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (2007), how did moral absolutists react when money was added to a taboo deal?
options: They showed more anger and more support for violence.
They showed less anger and less support for violence.
They showed no change in anger or support for violence.
They accepted the deal once the amount offered was large enough.
simple.why: For moral absolutists, Taboo+ raised anger and disgust and raised support for violence compared with the plain taboo deal. Money backfired for them.

college.stem: In the studies of Iranians who treat their nuclear program as a sacred value (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), how do added economic funds and added sanctions differ as manipulations?
options: Funds add a benefit for accepting the deal, while sanctions add a cost for refusing the deal.
Funds and sanctions both add only symbolic recognition, with no economic consequences attached.
Sanctions are an extra financial reward that participants' country receives for accepting the deal.
Funds directly change who holds a sacred value, while sanctions leave the deal itself unchanged.
college.why: An incentive (economic funds) makes accepting more rewarding, while a disincentive (sanctions) makes refusing more costly. The studies asked how such monetary pressures affect people holding a sacred value.

simple.stem: What question did the Iranian nuclear-program studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009) investigate?
options: Whether incentives or sanctions could get Iranians who hold the program sacred to compromise.
Whether Iranians could accurately recall the details of past nuclear agreements.
Whether Iranians preferred nuclear energy to nuclear weapons when asked directly.
Whether Israeli settlers would give up land in exchange for a large yearly cash payment.
simple.why: The studies tested whether Iranians who treat the nuclear program as a sacred value would respond to incentives or disincentives to compromise. The land question belongs to Ginges and colleagues (2007).

college.stem: In the online Farsi study of 1,997 Iranian participants (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), people were asked, “What do you think about Iran giving up its nuclear energy/weapons?” Which answer marked a sacred value?
options: This shouldn't be done no matter how great the consequences.
This should be done only if the benefits of stopping the program are great enough.
I do not object to Iran doing this at all.
I think this definitely needs to happen soon.
college.why: Only the answer refusing regardless of consequences counted as a sacred value (14% for energy, 13% for weapons). Accepting the deal if the benefits are great enough is a consequence-based position.

simple.stem: In the Iranian nuclear-program studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), which participants were counted as holding a sacred value?
options: Those who said giving it up shouldn't happen no matter the consequences.
Those who said giving it up should happen only for great enough benefits.
Those who said they did not object to Iran giving it up.
Those who said giving up the program definitely needs to happen.
simple.why: Participants who answered that the program should not be given up no matter how great the consequences were treated as holding a sacred value. Wanting enough benefits first is not sacred-value thinking.

college.stem: The Iranian scenarios (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009) crossed program type (nuclear energy vs. nuclear weapons) with deal type (Taboo, Taboo+, Taboo−). Which description of the design is accurate?
options: It has six conditions; Taboo+ adds $40 billion in funds and Taboo− adds sanctions if Iran refuses.
It has three conditions, because program type was a dependent variable rather than a manipulation.
It has six conditions; Taboo+ adds more sanctions and Taboo− adds $40 billion in funds.
It has two conditions, because every deal type offered exactly the same set of terms.
college.why: A 2 × 3 design gives six conditions. Taboo+ adds $40 billion from the United Nations, and Taboo− adds the threat of extra UN sanctions if Iran does not accept.

simple.stem: In the basic Taboo deal of the Iranian studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), what would Israel do in return for Iran giving up its program?
options: Israel would also give up its program and surrender its facilities to the UN.
Israel would pay Iran $40 billion in economic funds in exchange for the deal.
Israel would apologize for all the past wrongs done to Iran.
Israel would lift all of its own sanctions against Iran.
simple.why: In the Taboo deal, Israel would give up its own nuclear energy or weapons program and surrender its facilities to the UN. The $40 billion came from the UN, and only in Taboo+.

college.stem: In the nuclear-energy results of the Iranian studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), how did participants holding a sacred value respond to Taboo+ and Taboo− compared with the plain Taboo deal?
options: Both additions lowered approval and raised expected anger, with the added funds producing the most anger.
Both additions raised approval above the plain deal and removed nearly all expected anger.
Neither addition changed their approval, which stayed as high as that of participants without a sacred value.
Added funds raised their approval, while added sanctions lowered approval and increased expected anger.
college.why: For sacred-value participants, approval dropped from about 2.9 (Taboo) to about 1.9 (Taboo+) and 2.3 (Taboo−), and anger rose from about 3.2 to about 4.6 and 3.9. Funds did not raise approval.

simple.stem: In the nuclear-energy results of the Iranian studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), how did participants without a sacred value respond?
options: They gave fairly high approval and low anger to all three deals.
They gave low approval and high anger to all three deals.
They approved only the deal that added economic funds.
They approved only the deal that added extra sanctions.
simple.why: Participants without a sacred value gave approval of about 4.5–4.8 and anger of about 2.2 across all three deals. The big shifts appeared only in the sacred-value group.

college.stem: A researcher wants to show that ease of recall, not true frequency, drives judgments of probability. Which design most directly tests this?
options: Keep two events equally frequent, make one more distinctive or more often recalled, then collect probability judgments.
Change both frequency and exposure together, then credit any difference in judgment to availability alone.
Have participants pick an occupation from a personality sketch without ever measuring how easily any relevant instance is recalled.
Count the conjunctions in a sentence and treat that count as a measure of how accessible memories are.
college.why: Distinctiveness and repeated retrieval can make an event more available without changing its frequency, so holding frequency constant isolates availability. Changing both together confounds the two.

simple.stem: Which factors can make an event easier to remember, and so seem more probable?
options: Distinctiveness, emotional salience, and how often it is encoded or retrieved.
Its actual frequency in the population, and nothing else about the event at all.
How well it matches the typical member of a category.
Whether it combines two separate events into a single one.
simple.why: Distinctiveness, emotional salience and frequency of encoding or retrieval make events stand out in memory, which feeds the availability heuristic. Category match is representativeness.

college.stem: A respondent can define a base rate correctly but ignores it after hearing a description that fits a category. How does this explanation differ from an availability account?
options: Category membership is judged by resemblance to a typical member, not by how easily instances are recalled.
The judgment rests on counting memorable news stories about each group and using their ease of retrieval as the cue.
The judgment depends only on which event occurred most recently in a list the person recalls.
The judgment follows the rule that a conjunction cannot exceed the probability of either part.
college.why: Ignoring a base rate because a description fits a category is representativeness, which relies on similarity. Availability relies on how easily instances come to mind, as with memorable news stories.

simple.stem: Which situation shows the representativeness heuristic rather than availability?
options: Guessing that a quiet, bookish man is a librarian rather than a farmer.
Thinking plane crashes are common after seeing vivid news coverage of one.
Thinking more words start with r because those words come to mind easily.
Thinking botulism is a common killer because its deaths make headlines.
simple.why: Judging Robert a librarian because he resembles one is representativeness. The other three judge probability by how easily instances come to mind, which is availability.

college.stem: When judging whether descriptive information about Jack has displaced the base rate, which fact must stay in view?
options: The group still contains 70 lawyers and 30 engineers after Jack's personality description is added.
Jack's stated age of 45 should be read as the probability that he is an engineer.
Jack's hobbies should be counted as extra engineers and added to the group total.
The group must be redefined to hold only engineers before any judgment about Jack's occupation can be made.
college.why: The description changes what people attend to, not the numbers: there are still 70 lawyers and 30 engineers. Base-rate neglect is an error precisely because that information remains available.

simple.stem: In the Jack problem, what does the description of Jack change?
options: What people focus on, but not the 70-to-30 makeup of the group.
The group itself, so that most members are now engineers.
Nothing at all about how people answer the question.
The group itself, so that it now contains only lawyers.
simple.why: The description shifts attention to Jack's engineer-like traits, but the group still has 70 lawyers and 30 engineers. People's answers do change: they say Jack is an engineer.

college.stem: Picture all bank tellers as one circle, with a smaller circle of feminist bank tellers inside it. What does this set relationship settle about the Linda problem?
options: The joint event cannot be more probable than being a bank teller, however well Linda fits the added description.
The smaller circle is more probable, because a more specific description always contains more people than a general one.
Linda cannot possibly be a bank teller, because she does not fit the typical bank teller.
The two circles are unrelated, because sharing one condition cannot limit who belongs to each.
college.why: Every feminist bank teller is inside the bank-teller circle, so the conjunction cannot exceed the single event. That holds regardless of how well the description fits.

simple.stem: What did most people choose in the Linda problem?
options: Most chose that Linda is a bank teller and a feminist.
Most chose that Linda is simply a bank teller.
Most said both options were equally likely for Linda.
Most refused to choose because the description was vague.
simple.why: 82% picked “bank teller and active in the feminist movement,” violating the conjunction rule. The single event, bank teller, is at least as probable.

college.stem: A person picks the larger hospital because it delivers more boys over the year. Which correction addresses the hospital question as it was asked?
options: The outcome is days above a percentage cutoff, so compare how variable daily proportions are, not yearly totals.
The outcome is the yearly count of boys, so the percentage cutoff can be dropped as irrelevant.
The smaller hospital must have a different underlying sex ratio, since it has fewer births per day.
Neither hospital can exceed half boys on any day, since the population proportion is one half.
college.why: More births can mean more boys in absolute terms while producing fewer extreme daily percentages. The question is about daily proportions crossing 60%, which vary more in small samples.

simple.stem: Why is “the larger hospital” the wrong answer to the hospital problem?
options: Larger daily samples stay closer to 50% boys, so extreme days are rarer.
Larger hospitals keep less accurate records of the babies who are born there each day.
Larger hospitals deliver fewer boys than girls over a full year.
Larger hospitals never have a day with more boys than girls.
simple.why: Larger samples are more representative of the population, so the larger hospital rarely strays above 60% boys. The smaller hospital records more such days.

college.stem: Which finding would most directly support the claim that stereotypes produce illusory correlations?
options: Attention and recall favor stereotype-consistent behaviors, and the perceived link exceeds the actual relationship.
Every behavior receives equal attention from the observer, and the perceived link matches the observed relationship exactly.
The observer never notices or remembers any behavior performed by members of the group.
The perceived link appears only when the group happens to contain more than thirty people.
college.why: The proposed mechanism is selective attention to stereotypical behaviors, which makes them more available and inflates the perceived correlation. Equal attention with an accurate link would show no illusion.

simple.stem: How can a stereotype create an illusory correlation?
options: People pay extra attention to behaviors that fit the stereotype.
People record every behavior of the group with equal care.
People forget every behavior that fits the stereotype.
People form stereotypes only about very large groups.
simple.why: A stereotype draws attention to matching behaviors, making them more available and creating an illusory correlation that reinforces the stereotype.

college.stem: In the study by Lord and colleagues (1979), supporters and opponents of capital punishment read the same article, and each side discounted the parts that disagreed with it. Which concept best describes this?
options: Myside bias, a tendency to evaluate evidence in a way biased toward one's own opinions.
The conjunction rule, since the article combined two separate claims about punishment.
The law of large numbers, since the two sides formed samples of different sizes.
Expected utility theory, since each person maximized a monetary payoff for agreeing.
college.why: Myside bias is the tendency to generate and evaluate evidence in a way biased toward one's own opinions and attitudes. The other concepts concern probability or payoffs, not attitude-driven evaluation.

simple.stem: What is the myside bias?
options: Evaluating evidence in a way that favors your own opinions.
Judging events as likely when they are easy to remember.
Ignoring base rates when a description fits a category.
Choosing the option with the highest expected payoff.
simple.why: Myside bias, a type of confirmation bias, is generating and evaluating evidence in a way biased toward one's own opinions and attitudes.

college.stem: In the 2, 4, 6 number-rule task, which kind of test triple gives more information than another triple increasing by two?
options: A triple such as 1, 5, 20, which could separate “increasing by two” from “any increasing numbers.”
Another triple chosen only because it fits every feature of the current increasing-by-two hypothesis.
A request that the experimenter stop saying whether each triple fits the rule or not.
A decision to announce the current hypothesis as correct without considering any other rule.
college.why: A triple that the narrow hypothesis forbids but the broader rule allows can reveal that the narrow rule is wrong. More confirming triples leave the two hypotheses indistinguishable.

simple.stem: What is confirmation bias?
options: Looking for evidence that supports your hypothesis and overlooking evidence against it.
Testing your hypothesis by deliberately searching for evidence that could prove it wrong.
Changing your hypothesis every time you receive any new feedback.
Judging an event as likely because it resembles a typical case.
simple.why: Confirmation bias is the tendency to selectively look for information that conforms to our hypothesis and overlook information against it. Seeking disconfirming evidence is the opposite strategy.

college.stem: A person describing the jellybean choice says only “seven red beans versus one red bean.” What information is missing for comparing the two bowls?
options: The total number of beans in each bowl, needed to compare chances of 7/100 and 1/10.
The age of the person who filled the bowls, which sets all of the drawing probabilities.
The total number of dollars earned by every participant over the whole experiment.
Whether the color red was named using two separate adjectives combined together.
college.why: The chance of winning depends on the number of red beans relative to the total in the bowl. Seven of 100 is worse than one of 10 even though seven is the larger count.

simple.stem: In the jellybean study, which bowl gave the better chance of drawing a red bean?
options: The bowl with 1 red bean out of 10.
The bowl with 7 red beans out of 100.
Both bowls gave exactly the same chance.
Neither bowl contained any red beans at all.
simple.why: One in 10 is a 10% chance, while 7 in 100 is only 7%. Most participants nonetheless chose the 7-in-100 bowl.

college.stem: In Ritov and Baron's (1999) convoy dilemma, 12% of respondents would not reroute the convoy even if only 1 person at the first camp would die while 1,000 were saved. Which account does this response most directly contradict?
options: One in which decisions are determined solely by maximizing the net number of lives saved.
One in which the first camp receives no food after the convoy has been rerouted.
One in which decisions can involve considerations beyond the numerical balance of outcomes.
One in which the convoy is able to choose between two different refugee camps.
college.why: With only one life lost against 1,000 saved, a pure net-lives calculation strongly favors rerouting, so refusing contradicts that account. It is consistent with decisions involving other considerations.

simple.stem: In Ritov and Baron's (1999) convoy dilemma, what did 12% of respondents say?
options: They would not reroute even if only one person would die.
They would reroute even if 500 people at the first camp died.
They would refuse to answer the question about the convoy.
They would send half of the trucks to each of the camps.
simple.why: 12% said they would not change the convoy's route even if only one person in the first camp would die. Such refusals show that outcome counts alone do not drive these choices.

college.stem: Someone summarizes the results of Tetlock and colleagues (2000) as “saving Johnny affects outrage equally in both tradeoff types.” Which observation contradicts this summary?
options: The gap between saving and not saving Johnny is large under taboo but nearly absent under tragic.
The tragic condition has no outcome in which any child receives a liver transplant at all.
The taboo condition includes no money and so cannot be compared with the tragic condition.
Every bar in the results shows exactly the same outrage rating across all of the conditions.
college.why: Under taboo, outrage was about 5.4 versus 2.4 for not saving versus saving Johnny; under tragic, both were near 3.8. The outcome's effect depends on tradeoff type.

simple.stem: In Tetlock and colleagues' (2000) tragic tradeoff, how did outrage compare for saving versus not saving Johnny?
options: Outrage was about the same whether or not Johnny was saved.
Outrage was much higher when Johnny was not saved.
Outrage was much higher when Johnny was saved.
There was no outrage at all in either case.
simple.why: In the tragic tradeoff, outrage was similar (around 3.7–3.8) for both outcomes, because another child also needed the liver. The large gap appeared only in the taboo tradeoff.

college.stem: In the results of Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (2007), how did responses to the Symbolic offer differ from responses to adding money to a taboo deal?
options: The Symbolic offer lowered anger and support for violence, while added money raised both among moral absolutists.
The Symbolic offer was the same yearly payment as Taboo+, only stated in a different currency.
Both additions raised anger and support for violence by equal amounts in every participant group.
Neither addition changed any substantive term of the agreement, so responses were identical across all of the offers.
college.why: Compared with the taboo deal, the Symbolic offer produced less anger or disgust and less support for violence, whereas Taboo+ increased both among moral absolutists. Symbolic recognition and money engage different kinds of value.

simple.stem: In the results of Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (2007), what happened when Israel's side of the deal included recognition and an apology?
options: Anger and support for violence went down compared with the taboo deal.
Anger and support for violence went up compared with the taboo deal.
Anger went down, but support for violence rose sharply compared with the taboo deal.
Nothing changed, because symbolic gestures had no effect at all.
simple.why: The Symbolic offer lowered anger or disgust and dropped support for violence below zero, compared with the taboo deal. Money had the opposite effect for moral absolutists.

college.stem: A non-absolutist participant in the study by Ginges and colleagues (2007) strongly opposes a proposed agreement. Why would it be wrong to call this person indifferent just because the issue is not sacred to them?
options: Non-absolutists can strongly oppose compromise while still letting benefits and consequences shape their judgment.
Lacking a sacred value means that a person cannot hold any strong opinion, positive or negative, about the disputed issue.
Everyone who dislikes an agreement refuses it regardless of every possible consequence.
Moral absolutism is set by a person's group membership rather than by their own answers.
college.why: Non-absolutists had strong preferences against compromise but did not regard the issues as sacred. The difference from absolutists is about trading off consequences, not about caring.

simple.stem: In the study by Ginges and colleagues (2007), what was true of non-absolutists?
options: They strongly opposed compromise but did not treat the issues as sacred.
They had no opinion at all about the disputed issues.
They refused any compromise on the issues, no matter how great the benefit offered.
They were all Palestinian students from one political group.
simple.why: Non-absolutists had strong preferences against compromise but did not regard the issues as sacred values. Refusing regardless of benefit describes moral absolutists.

college.stem: In the Iranian nuclear-program studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), which statement keeps the sacred-value measure separate from the dependent variables?
options: Refusal regardless of consequences identified a sacred value, while approval, anger, and misleadingness measured reactions.
Approval alone determined how many participants were included, while all of the other responses were unrelated filler items.
Every participant held a sacred value, simply because the study was conducted in Farsi.
The number 1,997 gives the year the study was run rather than the number of participants.
college.why: The sacred-value measure sorted participants by whether they would refuse no matter the consequences; approval, expected anger and perceived misleadingness were the dependent variables. The study had 1,997 participants.

simple.stem: What were the dependent variables in the Iranian nuclear-program studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009)?
options: Approval of the deal, expected public anger, and whether it seemed misleading.
How much money each participant would personally accept to give up the nuclear program.
How quickly participants could recall the details of each deal.
Whether participants spoke Farsi or English at home with family.
simple.why: The dependent variables were people's approval, people's anger and a misleading rating. Sacred-value status was measured separately.

college.stem: In the Iranian nuclear scenarios (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), what exactly were participants asked when anger was measured?
options: Whether people would be angry if the Iranian government approved such a deal.
How angry they themselves had felt after seeing an unrelated news article.
How many sanctions the United Nations had already imposed on Iran.
Whether nuclear facilities produce a measurable physical anger response in workers.
college.why: The anger question asked whether people would be angry if the Iranian government approved the deal. It is separate from personal approval and from the misleading question.

simple.stem: In the Iranian nuclear scenarios (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), which question measured anger?
options: If the government approves the deal, will people be angry?
Do you personally approve of this deal being made?
If this deal is really proposed, is it misleading?
Should Iran give up its program no matter what?
simple.why: Anger was measured by asking whether people would be angry if the Iranian government approved the deal. The other questions measured approval, misleadingness, or sacred-value status.

college.stem: In the nuclear-energy results of the Iranian studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), participants without a sacred value showed similar low anger across all three deals, while those with a sacred value were angriest when funds were added. Which conclusion stays within these observations?
options: Reactions to economic additions depend on sacred-value status, at least for energy approval and anger.
The weapons results and misleading ratings must show exactly the same values as the energy results.
Every Iranian participant regards nuclear energy as a sacred value that cannot be traded away.
Adding funds raised approval among sacred-value participants above the level for the plain deal.
college.why: The energy results show sacred-value status changing reactions to added funds and sanctions. They do not report weapons or misleading ratings, only 14% held a sacred value for energy, and funds lowered approval in that group.

simple.stem: In the nuclear-energy results of the Iranian studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), which deal made sacred-value participants angriest?
options: The Taboo+ deal, which added $40 billion in economic funds.
The Taboo deal, with no funds or sanctions added at all.
The Taboo− deal, which added the threat of extra UN sanctions.
All three deals produced exactly the same amount of anger.
simple.why: Anger among sacred-value participants was highest for Taboo+ (about 4.6), then Taboo− (about 3.9), then plain Taboo (about 3.2).

college.stem: Which comparison best isolates the effect of adding an economic reward to the proposed nuclear deal in the Iranian studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009)?
options: Taboo versus Taboo+ for the same program type and sacred-value status, keeping the reciprocal deal in both.
Energy under Taboo versus weapons under Taboo−, crediting every single difference between them to the added funds alone.
The number of participants versus the number of deal types, calling the gap an approval effect.
Approval of the deal versus whether a participant speaks Farsi, without changing the offer at all.
college.why: Taboo+ is the Taboo deal plus $40 billion in funds, so comparing them with program type and sacred-value status held constant leaves the money as the only difference.

simple.stem: In the Iranian studies (Dehghani, Atran et al., 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al., 2009), what did the Taboo+ deal add to the basic Taboo deal?
options: The United Nations would give Iran $40 billion in economic funds.
The United Nations would impose additional sanctions if Iran refused.
Israel would apologize to Iran for all of its past wrongs.
Iran would be allowed to keep its nuclear weapons program.
simple.why: Taboo+ added $40 billion in UN economic funds to the reciprocal Taboo deal. Extra sanctions for refusing defined Taboo−.
